title: The Laplace Transform

blocks.html: The Laplace transform turns a function of time into a function of a new variable $s$. Its power, which you will see in the next topics, is that it turns derivatives into multiplication by $s$, so differential equations become algebra. It is built from an improper integral, and most table entries come from integration by parts.
$$\mathcal{L}\{f\}(s) = F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}f(t)\,dt,$$ defined for the $s$ where the integral converges. The transform is linear: $\mathcal{L}\{af + bg\} = aF + bG$.

For $e^{at}$: $\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s - a)t}\,dt$ $= \left[-\frac{e^{-(s - a)t}}{s - a}\right]_0^{\infty} = \frac{1}{s - a}$, provided $s > a$ so the exponential dies out. For powers, integrating by parts gives $\mathcal{L}\{t^{n}\} = \frac{n}{s}\mathcal{L}\{t^{n-1}\}$, and repeating down to $\mathcal{L}\{1\} = \frac{1}{s}$ gives $\frac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$. For sine and cosine, put $a = ib$: $\frac{1}{s - ib} = \frac{s + ib}{s^{2} + b^{2}}$, and by Euler's formula the real and imaginary parts are the transforms of $\cos bt$ and $\sin bt$.

blocks.title: From the definition
blocks.q: Find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{3t}\}$ and say where it is valid.
steps: For $s > 3$ the integrand decays and the integral is $\frac{1}{s - 3}$; for $s \le 3$ it diverges.

blocks.title: A pulse
blocks.q: Find the transform of $f(t) = 2$ for $0 \le t < 3$ and $f(t) = 0$ for $t \ge 3$.

blocks.html: Treating $s$ and $t$ alike. The integral is over $t$, so $s$ acts as a constant inside it and survives in the answer, while $t$ disappears. Also keep the convergence condition in mind: $\frac{1}{s - 3}$ represents $\mathcal{L}\{e^{3t}\}$ only for $s > 3$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The integrand $te^{-st}$ for $f(t) = t$. The shaded area is $F(s) = \frac{1}{s^{2}}$. Larger $s$ squeezes the area toward 0; smaller $s$ spreads it out.

blocks.html: Which functions have a transform? It is enough that $f$ is piecewise continuous and of exponential order: $|f(t)| \le Me^{at}$ for large $t$. Then the integral converges for every $s > a$, because the factor $e^{-st}$ wins. Polynomials, exponentials, sines and step functions all qualify; $e^{t^{2}}$ grows too fast and has no transform. For such functions $F(s) \to 0$ as $s \to \infty$, so an expression like $\frac{s^{2}}{s + 1}$ is not the transform of any ordinary function.
